questions.stem: Which definition of the term allele is correct?
options: A pair of matching chromosomes in a cell
The physical trait produced by a gene
One of the alternative forms of a gene
The position of a gene on a chromosome
questions.explanation: Alleles are different versions of the same gene, such as the alleles for normal and deficient enzyme in PKU. The position of a gene is its locus, and the trait is the phenotype.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say a person is heterozygous for a gene?
options: They show the recessive form of the trait
They have two different alleles of the gene
They have two identical alleles of the gene
They have only one copy of the gene in total
questions.explanation: Heterozygous means carrying two different alleles, for example Pp. Homozygous means carrying two identical alleles, PP or pp.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a genotype and a phenotype?
options: Genotype is the trait that is expressed; phenotype is the alleles a person has
Genotype applies only to dominant alleles; phenotype only to recessive alleles
Genotype is found in body cells; phenotype is found only in the gametes
Genotype is the alleles a person has; phenotype is the trait that is expressed
questions.explanation: The genotype is the combination of alleles, such as IAi, and the phenotype is the observable characteristic, such as blood group A. Phenotype can also be influenced by the environment.

questions.stem: How is Huntington's disease inherited?
options: Co-dominant
Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
questions.explanation: One copy of the Huntington's allele on an autosome is enough to cause the disease. PKU is autosomal recessive and haemophilia is X-linked recessive.

questions.stem: A man heterozygous for Huntington's disease (Hh) has children with a woman who does not carry the allele (hh). What is the probability that each child will inherit the disease?
questions.explanation: The cross Hh × hh gives Hh and hh in equal proportions, so each child has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting the dominant allele and developing the disease.

questions.stem: Symptoms of Huntington's disease usually appear in middle adulthood. Why does this allow the allele to be passed on despite its severe effects?
options: Many people have already had children before they know they carry the allele
The allele is recessive, so it is hidden in carriers who never show symptoms
The allele mutates back to the normal form in people who have children
The allele is found only in mitochondria, so it is always passed on by mothers
questions.explanation: Because onset is usually after the reproductive years have begun, a person may pass on the dominant allele before symptoms appear. This is one reason predictive testing raises difficult decisions.

questions.stem: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. What causes the condition?
options: Lack of a clotting factor needed to form fibrin in the blood
An extra copy of chromosome 21 in each of the body's cells
Lack of a working enzyme to break down the amino acid phenylalanine
Production of too much insulin by the pancreas after meals
questions.explanation: People with PKU are homozygous for an allele that gives a faulty phenylalanine-processing enzyme, so phenylalanine builds up and can damage the developing brain. A lack of a clotting factor causes haemophilia.

questions.stem: Two parents who are both carriers of PKU (Pp) have a child. What is the probability that the child has PKU?
questions.explanation: Pp × Pp gives PP : Pp : pp in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1, so 1 in 4 children are expected to be homozygous recessive and have PKU.

questions.stem: Two carriers of PKU (Pp) have a child who does not have PKU. What is the probability that this child is a carrier?
questions.explanation: Among unaffected offspring of Pp × Pp, the genotypes are PP, Pp and Pp, so two out of three are carriers. The common slip is to use 1/2 from the whole Punnett square, which includes the affected pp child.

questions.stem: Newborns in Australia are routinely screened for PKU with a heel-prick blood test. Why is early detection so valuable?
options: The faulty allele can be removed from the baby's cells if found early
Early detection allows a blood transfusion that cures the condition
Antibiotics given in the first week of life kill the cause of PKU
A diet low in phenylalanine from early infancy can prevent brain damage
questions.explanation: PKU cannot be cured, but limiting phenylalanine in the diet from early infancy keeps blood levels low and allows normal brain development. It is a genetic, not infectious, condition.

questions.stem: A woman with PKU who has followed a strict diet in childhood plans a pregnancy. Why is she advised to resume a low-phenylalanine diet before conceiving?
options: Phenylalanine in her diet would turn the foetus into a carrier of PKU
Without the diet her eggs would not contain the gene for the enzyme
High phenylalanine in her blood can cross the placenta and harm the foetus
The diet changes her allele to the dominant form so the baby is unaffected
questions.explanation: If her blood phenylalanine is high, it reaches the foetus and can damage its development regardless of the foetus's genotype. Diet affects the environment of the foetus, not the alleles it inherits.

questions.stem: Why are ABO blood groups an example of multiple alleles?
options: Many different genes on several chromosomes add together to give the blood group
The gene has only two alleles, but each one has a strong effect on blood type
There are three alleles of the gene in the population: IA, IB and i
Each person carries three alleles of the gene, one on each of three chromosomes
questions.explanation: A gene with more than two alleles in the population shows multiple alleles. Each person still carries only two of them, one on each homologous chromosome.

questions.stem: A person has genotype IA IB. What is their blood group, and what does it show?
options: Group AB, showing that IA and IB are co-dominant
Group A, showing that IA is dominant over IB
Group B, showing that IB is dominant over IA
Group O, showing that the two alleles cancel out
questions.explanation: Both alleles are fully expressed, so both A and B antigens appear on the red cells. When both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed, they are co-dominant.

questions.stem: Which genotype gives blood group O?
options: IB i
IA IB
ii
IA i
questions.explanation: The i allele is recessive to both IA and IB, so only a person homozygous for i has group O, with no A or B antigens.

questions.stem: A man with blood group A and a woman with blood group B have a child with blood group O. What are the parents' genotypes?
options: Man IA IA; woman IB IB
Man IA IA; woman IB i
Man IA IB; woman ii
Man IA i; woman IB i
questions.explanation: A group O child is ii and must have received an i from each parent, so both parents are heterozygous. A man with group A must carry IA, and the woman with group B must carry IB.

questions.stem: What proportion of children from the cross IA i × IB i are expected to have blood group AB?
questions.explanation: The cross gives IA IB, IA i, IB i and ii in equal proportions, so 1/4 are AB, 1/4 A, 1/4 B and 1/4 O. All four blood groups are possible from this cross.

questions.stem: A woman with blood group O and a man with blood group AB have children. Which blood groups are possible among their children?
options: AB and O only
A, B, AB and O
O only
A and B only
questions.explanation: ii × IA IB gives IA i and IB i only, so children have group A or group B. None can be AB or O, because each child receives i from the mother and either IA or IB from the father.

questions.stem: In a paternity dispute, a child has blood group AB and the mother has group A. Which man could not be the father?
options: A man with blood group O
A man with blood group B
A man with blood group AB
A man with genotype IB i
questions.explanation: The child (IA IB) received IA from the mother, so must have received IB from the father. A group O man (ii) has no IB allele, so he is excluded; blood groups can rule a man out but cannot prove he is the father.

questions.stem: Why are X-linked recessive conditions such as haemophilia much more common in males?
options: The Y chromosome carries a dominant allele that causes the condition
Females destroy the faulty allele during the formation of their eggs
Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed
Males have two X chromosomes, so they inherit twice as many faulty alleles
questions.explanation: A male has no second X to carry a normal allele, so one recessive allele on his X causes the condition. A female needs two copies, one on each X.

questions.stem: Using X^N for the normal allele and X^c for the red-green colour blindness allele, what is the genotype of a colour-blind man?
options: X^N Y
X^c X^c
X^N X^c
X^c Y
questions.explanation: Males are XY, so a colour-blind man carries the recessive allele on his single X. X^c X^c would be a colour-blind female, and X^N X^c a carrier female.

questions.stem: A woman who is a carrier of red-green colour blindness (X^B X^b) has children with a man with normal vision (X^B Y). What proportion of their sons are expected to be colour-blind?
options: All of them
questions.explanation: Every son receives Y from his father and one X from his mother; half the mother's eggs carry X^b, so half the sons are expected to be colour-blind.

questions.stem: For the same cross (X^B X^b × X^B Y), what is the probability that their next child is a colour-blind son?
questions.explanation: The chance of a son is 1/2 and the chance a son receives X^b is 1/2, so 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The answer 1/2 is the proportion among sons only, not among all children.

questions.stem: A man with haemophilia (X^h Y) has children with a woman who is homozygous normal (X^H X^H). What are the expected outcomes?
options: All daughters are carriers; no sons have haemophilia
All sons have haemophilia; no daughters are carriers
Half the sons have haemophilia; half the daughters are carriers
All children have haemophilia because the father has it
questions.explanation: Daughters receive the father's X^h and the mother's X^H, so all are carriers. Sons receive the father's Y and an X^H from the mother, so none are affected: a father cannot pass an X-linked allele to his sons.

questions.stem: Haemophilia A is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. What does the normal allele code for?
options: A protein needed for blood clotting (factor VIII)
The haemoglobin carried by red blood cells
The A antigen found on red blood cells
An enzyme that breaks down phenylalanine
questions.explanation: Haemophilia A results from a lack of functional clotting factor VIII, so blood clots very slowly. People with it are treated with replacement factor.

questions.stem: A colour-blind woman has children with a man with normal vision. What would you expect among their children?
options: All daughters colour-blind; all sons with normal vision
Half the sons and half the daughters colour-blind
No colour-blind children, because the father has normal vision
All sons colour-blind; all daughters carriers with normal vision
questions.explanation: The mother is X^b X^b, so every son gets X^b and is colour-blind. Daughters get X^B from the father as well as X^b from the mother, so they are carriers with normal vision.

questions.stem: In a standard pedigree chart, what does a shaded square represent?
options: A male who shows the trait
A female who shows the trait
A male carrier of the trait
A female who does not show the trait
questions.explanation: Squares represent males and circles females; shading means the individual shows (is affected by) the trait. Carriers are sometimes shown half-shaded or with a dot.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. What does this show about the trait?
options: It is dominant, and the daughter is a new carrier
It is recessive, and both parents are carriers
It is dominant, and both parents are homozygous
It is X-linked recessive, and the father is affected
questions.explanation: Unaffected parents with an affected child must both carry a hidden recessive allele. It cannot be X-linked recessive, because the daughter would need an affected father.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, two affected parents have an unaffected son. What can be concluded?
options: The trait is recessive, and the son is a carrier
The trait must be dominant rather than recessive
The trait is recessive, and both parents are carriers
The trait is X-linked recessive, and the mother is a carrier
questions.explanation: If the trait were recessive, two affected parents (aa × aa) could only have affected children. An unaffected child means the trait must be dominant; if it is autosomal, both parents are heterozygous.

questions.stem: A pedigree shows a trait in many males and few females; affected males have unaffected parents, and the trait is never passed from father to son. Which pattern fits best?
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
Mitochondrial
X-linked recessive
questions.explanation: An excess of affected males, transmission through unaffected carrier mothers and no father-to-son transmission are the hallmarks of X-linked recessive inheritance.

questions.stem: Why is a pedigree useful to a genetic counsellor?
options: It cures the disorder by identifying the person who first carried it
It shows the number of chromosomes in each person's body cells
It reveals the pattern of inheritance and helps estimate risks for future children
It shows the DNA sequence of the faulty allele in each family member
questions.explanation: Tracing a condition through generations shows whether it is dominant, recessive or sex-linked, from which the genotypes of relatives and the probabilities for future children can be worked out.

questions.stem: In a family with an autosomal dominant disorder, an affected woman (Aa) and an unaffected man have three unaffected children. What is the probability their fourth child will be affected?
questions.explanation: Each child is an independent event: Aa × aa gives a 1/2 chance every time, whatever happened to earlier children. Assuming earlier outcomes change the risk is a common error.

questions.stem: A couple from a family with cystic fibrosis have carrier screening before trying for a baby. What is the main purpose?
options: To cure any carriers by removing the allele from their reproductive cells
To find whether either of them already has symptoms of the disorder
To change the dominant allele in their eggs and sperm before conception
To find whether both carry the recessive allele and could have an affected child
questions.explanation: Carrier screening identifies people who carry one copy of a recessive allele. If both partners are carriers, each child has a 1 in 4 chance of being affected, which informs their decisions.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old whose parent has Huntington's disease is considering a predictive genetic test. Which is an ethical consideration rather than a scientific fact?
options: Whether the allele is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
Whether the test can detect the allele in a sample of blood
Whether the person has a 50% chance of having inherited the allele
Whether the person wants to know their status when there is no cure
questions.explanation: Choosing whether to learn of an incurable future illness depends on personal values and consequences for wellbeing, relationships and relatives. The other statements can be settled by evidence.

questions.stem: Genetic test results can reveal information about a person's relatives as well as themselves. Which concern does this raise?
options: Cost: relatives must pay for the person's test before it is done
Privacy: relatives may learn of risks they did not choose to find out
Accuracy: tests on one person always give false results for relatives
Safety: a blood sample from one person can infect their relatives
questions.explanation: Because relatives share alleles, one person's result can imply risks for siblings, parents or children, raising questions of privacy, consent and whether to share the information.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a limitation of genetic screening for inherited disorders?
options: Screening alters the alleles of the people tested, so it cannot be used in pregnancy
Screening results are always certain and so give no room for personal decisions
A positive result may cause anxiety and difficult choices, even where no treatment exists
Screening tests can only detect disorders after symptoms have already appeared
questions.explanation: Screening can identify risk before symptoms or before conception, but knowledge can bring distress and decisions about relationships, pregnancy and insurance. Tests do not alter a person's alleles.

questions.stem: A family history suggests that a disorder is inherited. Which representation would best show the pattern across three generations?
options: A karyotype
A Punnett square
A DNA sequence
A pedigree chart
questions.explanation: A pedigree traces a trait through generations of a family. A Punnett square predicts the offspring of one cross, and a karyotype shows the chromosomes of one person.

questions.stem: What is a recessive allele?
options: An allele expressed in the phenotype only when two copies are present
An allele expressed in the phenotype whenever one copy is present
An allele found only on the Y chromosome of males
An allele that always causes a genetic disorder
questions.explanation: A recessive allele is masked by a dominant allele in a heterozygote, so it shows only in the homozygous state, as in PKU. Many recessive alleles are harmless.

questions.stem: What is meant by an autosomal allele?
options: An allele on one of the 22 pairs of chromosomes that are not sex chromosomes
An allele on the X chromosome that is expressed only in females
An allele found in mitochondrial DNA and passed on by the mother
An allele on the Y chromosome that is passed from father to son
questions.explanation: Autosomes are chromosome pairs 1 to 22, which are the same in both sexes, so autosomal traits affect males and females equally. Alleles on the X or Y are sex-linked.
